nameStory: Toothcup gets its intriguing name from the tiny triangular sepals (the green parts behind the petals) that have narrow, pointed appendages sticking out like little teeth around each small flower. When you look closely at the flowers, these tooth-like projections create a distinctive cup shape that early botanists thought resembled a toothed rim.
description: Toothcup is a delicate aquatic or semi-aquatic plant that thrives in shallow water and muddy shores throughout New England. This branching herb grows up to about 16 inches long, with slender stems that may float on water or creep along wet ground. Its small white to pinkish flowers are barely noticeable unless you look closely, but the plant's neat, opposite leaves and preference for water's edge make it distinctive once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white to pale pink flowers, usually with four petals, nestled singly where leaves meet the stem; look for the distinctive triangular sepals with narrow, tooth-like projections that give the plant its name

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped to oval leaves up to 2 inches long, arranged in opposite pairs that alternate at right angles to each other up the stem, creating a neat cross-pattern when viewed from above

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing, branching stems that may float on water surface or sprawl across wet mud, feeling somewhat succulent and flexible to the touch

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in or very close to water - stream edges, pond margins, or wet ditches where the soil stays consistently moist or muddy

habitat: Look for toothcup along the muddy or sandy edges of ponds, streams, and slow-moving waterways throughout New England. It thrives in shallow water and wet soils of marshes, irrigation ditches, and the fluctuating water zones of lakes where water levels rise and fall seasonally.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins to emerge from muddy substrates as water warms, with fresh green shoots appearing along shorelines.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and flowering season, when the tiny white to pink flowers are most visible and the plant reaches its full branching growth.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back as temperatures cool, though some may persist in protected areas or where water temperatures remain warmer.
seasonality.winter: Mostly dormant with little visible above-ground growth, persisting through seeds and possibly root systems in milder areas.

funFact: Toothcup is popular among aquarium enthusiasts who grow it as a delicate underwater plant, where its neat, opposite leaves and branching pattern create beautiful miniature underwater forests in fish tanks!
confusionNotes: With only 16 recorded observations in New England, toothcup might be confused with other small water-edge plants, but its distinctive opposite leaf arrangement in perpendicular pairs and tiny flowers tucked into leaf joints set it apart from most wetland species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'lowland rotala' in some references, most New Englanders know this plant simply as toothcup - the rotala name is more commonly used by aquarium hobbyists and botanists.
compareHints: Toothcup is the only Rotala species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Within the loosestrife family, it differs from the more familiar purple loosestrife by being much smaller, having opposite (not whorled) leaves, and producing tiny individual flowers rather than showy flower spikes.
